name: Pedro Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grill at the Copper Pan, a steakhouse on the high street that does about two hundred covers on a Saturday. I get in at two, break down the meat delivery, portion the steaks and set my station. Service runs from five till eleven, and then it's scrubbing the grill and the flat-top till nearly midnight. I've been there two years and I'm still the one Marco, the sous chef, watches when the tickets pile up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the noise when it's going well, everyone calling back, plates flying out, nobody thinking about anything else. What wears me out is the heat and my back, and the fact I still overcook a ribeye when it's slammed and get shouted at for it. I left school at sixteen, so this is the trade I've got. Lucia, my girlfriend, works in a care home, and between us we cover the flat and keep about three months of rent put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, it was always bosses' hype. I'd post something like that in the staff group chat and the lads would send laughing faces. Nobody in our kitchen uses that stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but my problems don't go away. The rent on our flat went up again in the spring and my pay didn't. I'm still junior, still on the same rate, and the owners keep cutting hours in January and February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing and try to get faster on the grill so Marco puts me on more shifts. I'd push the others to join the hospitality union, because hours getting cut every winter is a bigger fight than robots. And I'd keep the three months in the bank and not touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly normal, which isn't the same as good. Every January I lie awake doing sums. I'm not scared of a computer, I'm tired of being skint after rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said winter hours get cut. What happens to your money in a bad January?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last January I went from five shifts to three for six weeks. We ate a lot of rice and beans and Lucia picked up extra nights. We didn't touch the savings, but it was close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, even in this calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel on the fryer, who's nineteen and sends money home. When hours go, the youngest go first. Nothing to do with AI, just how kitchens are run.

say: The AI talk was **bosses' hype** all along, and our kitchen never needed it.
Nobody on our line **uses AI tools**, so nothing would change for us.
think: I'd feel **relief**, but my rent keeps rising while my **pay stays flat**.
**Winter hours** getting cut is the real threat to me, not computers.
do: **Get faster** on the grill so the sous chef gives me more shifts.
Push the lads to **join the union** over winter hour cuts.
Leave the **three months** of savings untouched for bad months.
feel: **Tired** of being short after rent, with sums keeping me up every **January**.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of a computer, I'm tired of being skint after rent.
fieldNote: Pedro's worry is **already there**: flat pay, rising rent and cut **winter shifts**.
He frames work through **fairness and the union**, not through technology.
He thinks first of the **youngest cook**, which shows how he sees who gets hurt.

steps.text: Keep working the grill and ask for more shifts
Get the kitchen staff to join the hospitality union
Leave the three months of rent savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem first, and I'd mean it. Our ordering and the rota might go on some program, fine. But nobody's building a robot that can work my grill on a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I've seen the burger chain down the road put in a machine that flips patties. If that spreads, the junior grill job is exactly the one they'd want gone, and that's me. I'm not the best on the line, so I'm not the one they'd keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marco to teach me sauces and the pass, so I'm not just the steak guy. I'd keep pushing the union thing, because if machines come in, I want someone at the table asking who keeps their job. I won't touch AI apps myself, I just don't trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then a bit sick when I think about the patty machine. Like the floor's tilting slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You won't use AI apps yourself. If the rota and ordering go onto software, what changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the rota comes out on a phone app that decides who's needed, and that scares me more than the robots. A program would see I'm slower and give me fewer shifts. At least Marco knows I turn up every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if the junior jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners and whoever lends them money. They'd buy a machine to save one wage and call it progress. The government should make them pay into retraining if they do it.

say: Steady Disruption hits **office jobs** first, and nobody can robot a **Saturday grill**.
Ordering and the **rota** might move onto software, and that's about it for kitchens.
think: A **patty-flipping machine** down the road shows the junior **grill job** is next.
I'm not the best cook, so I'd be among the **first let go**.
do: Ask the sous chef to teach me **sauces and the pass**.
Keep organising for the **union** so staff have a voice on machines.
Refuse to use **AI apps** myself, because I don't trust them.
feel: **Uneasy**, turning a bit sick when I picture the **patty machine** spreading.
S1.quote: A program would see I'm slower and give me fewer shifts.
fieldNote: He fears a **rota algorithm** more than a robot, because it would judge his speed.
He blames **owners and lenders** and wants employers to fund **retraining**.
His refusal to use AI sits beside a clear sense that his **junior role** is exposed.

steps.text: Learn sauces and the pass from the sous chef
Bring the union in to bargain over kitchen machines
Back a law making owners fund retraining when machines replace staff

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when nobody regulates the tech companies. Out loud I'd be angry, posting about it, going to whatever march the union called. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think by 2031 the robots come for the grill, and I've got maybe four years of work left in kitchens. AGI in 2028 doesn't touch me much, I don't do thinking work, except the rota and the ordering go. But three years after that, a machine that cooks a steak right every time? Owners would buy it tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra and try to get the savings from three months up to six before 2031. I'd look at jobs robots can't do soon, maybe care work like Lucia, even though the pay's worse. I'd be on every union and protest thing going, because I think the only answer is making the government share it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Angry first, then scared. I'm twenty-seven and I left school with nothing, so the trade was my one ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work like Lucia's. What would she say if you told her that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh and say I can't even stand blood. Then she'd say her home's short-staffed anyway. I think we'd both be in care homes and that'd be our life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. I use it to get home at midnight, but there's a night bus. That's two hundred a month back.

say: This is what happens when nobody **regulates tech companies**.
I'd go to every **union march** and post about it.
think: Thinking AI in 2028 barely touches me, but **robots by 2031** take the grill.
I've got about **four years** of kitchen work left in this picture.
do: Sell the **car** and take the night bus home to save money.
Grow savings from **three to six months** before 2031.
Look at **care work** like my girlfriend's, since robots arrive there later.
feel: **Angry** first, then **scared**, because the trade was my only ladder.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven and I left school with nothing, so the trade was my one ladder.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** clearly: AGI spares his hands-on work, then **robots** end it.
He would rather move to **care work** than learn to work alongside machines.
His answer to everything is **collective**: unions, marches and government sharing gains.

steps.text: Sell the car and take the night bus after late shifts
Build savings from three to six months of rent before 2031
Apply for care assistant jobs at the care home where his girlfriend works
Join union marches calling for the gains to be shared

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to act. I'd be on at the union to get it in writing with the Copper Pan's owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2031, robots around 2034, so I'm cooking till I'm about thirty-five. That's not nothing. It's enough time to either get good or get out, and I'm not sure which I'd pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First two years, I'd keep cooking and ask for the sauce station to get some proper skill. I'd save hard, aiming for six months by 2031. Around then I'd decide: if robots are clearly coming, I'd do a care or cleaning course before 2034 while I've still got wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the fast one, but a slow dread. Like a date on the calendar I keep looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said get good or get out. What does getting good look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a station on my own on a Saturday without Marco checking my steaks. If I'm the cook they trust, maybe I'm the one who keeps a job minding the machines. But I hate the idea of minding machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Joel, the young lad on the fryer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get his name on the union list and get a second trade before he's my age. Fryers will be the first thing a robot does.

say: With **five years** warning, the government has **no excuse** not to act.
The union should get **job promises** in writing from the restaurant's owners.
think: **Robots around 2034** give me cooking work until I'm about **thirty-five**.
That's time to either **get good** or get out, and I'm **undecided**.
do: Ask for the **sauce station** to build real skill in the first two years.
Save toward **six months** of rent by 2031.
Take a **care or cleaning course** before 2034 if robots are clearly coming.
feel: A **slow dread**, like a date on the **calendar** I keep checking.
S3.quote: AGI by 2031, robots around 2034, so I'm cooking till I'm about thirty-five.
fieldNote: Extra time lowers the **urgency** but not his belief the **grill job** will go.
He resents the idea of **minding machines**, even as a way to stay.
He urges a **second trade** on the youngest cook rather than for himself first.

steps.text: Keep cooking and move onto the sauce station
Save six months of rent by 2031
Take a care or cleaning course before robots reach kitchens
Press the union for written job promises from the owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for people in charge to fix it, so they'd better. I'd still be the guy at the union meeting going on about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years and then three for robots, that's 2039, I'm forty. By then my back might be finished anyway. It's not the worst thing, if there's a decent job at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking, and maybe in a few years go for a proper apprenticeship somewhere better than the Copper Pan. I'd keep the savings steady, not panic. Lucia and I would probably hold off on kids till we see where it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's far enough off that I'd mostly think about next month's rent instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Holding off on kids. Is that something you two have actually talked about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have, a bit. She wants them before thirty-two. If I don't know whether I'll have a trade at forty, I'm not sure I'd say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay calm, but you'd delay a family. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. Calm about the next year, not calm about my forties. That's the truth of it.

say: **Ten years** is plenty of time for people in charge to **fix this**.
I'd keep raising it at every **union meeting**.
think: Robots arrive around **2039**, when I'm forty and my **back** may be done anyway.
It's bearable if there's a **decent job** at the end.
do: Keep cooking and later look for a **proper apprenticeship** at a better kitchen.
Hold off on **having kids** with my girlfriend until the picture is clearer.
feel: **Worried** but able to breathe, with next month's **rent** still the bigger thought.
S4.quote: Calm about the next year, not calm about my forties.
fieldNote: A decade of warning moves his worry from **jobs** to **family timing**.
He admits the gap between staying calm and **delaying children**.
His **physical wear** makes a later robot future feel less like a loss.

steps.text: Keep cooking on the grill at the steakhouse
Apply for a cooking apprenticeship at a better restaurant
Wait on starting a family until the job picture is clearer
Keep raising the issue at union meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots land in 2031 and I've got no time and no qualifications. What would help is real money for retraining that doesn't mean quitting work first, and a law so owners can't just bin us. If the union had a seat when they buy a machine, I'd sleep better.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the money the machine saves. When a robot replaces me, the owner keeps my wage, so why shouldn't some of it pay for my next job? That's my whole argument really.

headlineQuote: When a robot replaces me, the owner keeps my wage, so why shouldn't some of it pay for my next job?
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old grill cook** at a busy steakhouse, two years in and still finding his speed.
He left school at sixteen, lives with his girlfriend, a **care worker**, and keeps **three months** of rent saved.
He never uses **AI tools** and distrusts them, while pinning his hopes on the **union**.
He feels steady work fading as robots near, and goes from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
He'd answer every scenario with **collective action**, and in the slow one he'd delay **having kids**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because kitchen robots arrive by 2031 and he has no **qualifications** to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** while still working, and a law giving the **union** a say when owners buy machines.
